name: Nootropic stacks

card.summary: Combinations of cognitive-enhancing supplements and drugs that looksmaxxers use for focus, study and motivation, as part of building the mental side of self-improvement.
card.note: Some stack components are prescription or controlled drugs; supplement products have been found mislabeled.

quick.overview:
A nootropic stack is a combination of substances, from caffeine and L-theanine to racetams, herbal extracts and prescription stimulants, taken together for attention, memory, wakefulness and motivation. In looksmaxxing forums they are discussed under 'IQmaxxing' and study-focus threads, tied to the broader goal of self-improvement rather than directly to appearance.

The appearance link is indirect: people say better focus and energy help them stay consistent with training, school and routines. Reviews of 'smart drugs' in healthy people describe modest, dose-dependent effects for some stimulants and limited evidence for most supplements.
quick.how: Forum users compile lists of substances, ask which to add to a stack, and compare experiences. Common items mentioned include caffeine with L-theanine, omega-3, curcumin, Bacopa, creatine, racetams and wakefulness agents. Some prefer non-prescription items and avoid anything that might affect hormones or hair.
quick.risks: Reviews describe side effects, possible dependence with stimulants and long-term safety gaps for many compounds. Supplements can contain undeclared drugs and be mislabeled, and some components are controlled or prescription-only. People with medical conditions or on medication are generally advised by clinicians to consult a physician.

lead: Nootropic stacks are combinations of cognitive enhancers, often called 'smart drugs', that people take together aiming for better focus, memory, wakefulness or motivation. The term 'nootropic' was coined in 1972 by Corneliu Giurgea, who proposed criteria such as enhancing learning and memory with few side effects. [1]

In looksmaxxing communities they appear in study and 'lock in' threads. Users list the substances they already take, such as modafinil or noopept, ask what else to add, and trade views on over-the-counter versus prescription options. [3][4] The link to looks is a chain: better concentration and energy support consistent training, studying and routines.

Reviews of cognitive enhancers in healthy people report modest effects for some, dose-dependent for stimulants, and limited data for many supplements. [2][5] Medical bodies such as the AMA have discouraged prescribing them to healthy people. [1]

chain: Stack of supplements or drugs taken for focus and wakefulness
More consistent training, study and self-improvement routines
angle.text: People use stacks to concentrate better and keep up with routines that feed into physique, skin care and school. The effect on appearance is indirect and runs through habits rather than any change to the face or body.

paras: There is no globally accepted clinical definition of nootropic, and the term covers prescription drugs and dietary supplements. [1] Wikipedia lists stimulants such as caffeine and modafinil, cholinergics, racetams, herbs such as Bacopa monnieri and Ginkgo biloba, and nutrients including omega-3 fatty acids among the commonly named groups. [1] A 2022 review divided them into classical nootropics, brain-metabolism enhancers, cholinergic agents and plant extracts. [2]

Giurgea's 1972 definition followed work on piracetam at the Belgian company UCB in the 1960s. [1][6] Interest grew with stimulants such as modafinil and methylphenidate in the 1990s and with internet communities in the 2000s, and a 2021 review noted use among university students. [6][9]

Threads ask for stacks for 'wakefulness, focus, memory, and concentration for studying' and list items like modafinil and noopept. [3] Replies range from supplement lists to arguments that over-the-counter stimulants are weak, and some users say they avoid items thought to affect hair or growth hormone. [3][4]

A 2022 review of smart drugs in healthy individuals describes prevalence, putative benefits and possible harms, noting that effects in non-impaired people are not fully assessed. [5] A systematic review of plant-derived nootropics examined human cognition across domains. [7] Wikipedia notes that low-dose stimulants can improve some functions while high doses impair them, and that evidence for most supplements in healthy people is limited. [1]

Wikipedia reports concerns about adverse effects, psychological dependence, missing long-term data and supplements containing hidden drugs; the FDA warned manufacturers from 2010 to 2019 about unapproved products, and a 2021 study found five unapproved drugs in cognitive supplements. [1]

Human studies include reviews of cognitive enhancers in healthy people and students, a systematic review of plant-derived nootropics, and trials of individual products such as a randomized trial of guayusa and lion's mane extracts and one of an energy drink in gamers. [2][5][7][8][9] Studies of stacks as combined in forums were not found.

timeline.event: AMA discourages prescribing nootropics to healthy people. [1]
FDA and FTC warn about nootropic marketing claims. [1]

lore.intro: Nootropics are discussed on looksmax.org as tools for studying and motivation, often with competing views on prescription versus over-the-counter options. [3][4]

claims.claim: Prescription stimulants work and over-the-counter nootropics are 'cope'
claims.believers: One user says OTC stimulants give only slight energy with side effects and recommends a prescription instead. [4]
claims.experts: Reviews report dose-dependent effects for stimulants in healthy people and limited evidence for most supplements. [1][5]

claims.claim: A stack of supplements can improve focus for exams
claims.believers: A forum reply lists a multi-supplement stack and a caffeine-theanine pairing for studying. [3]
claims.experts: A systematic review of plant-derived nootropics examined human cognition effects. [7]
